questions.question: A training pod ignores SIGTERM for 30 seconds and then dies with exit code 137. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.model_answer: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM only to the process with PID 1 in the container. When the entrypoint is a shell script, the shell is PID 1 and it does not pass the signal on to python. After the grace period of 30 seconds Kubernetes sends SIGKILL, and the exit code is 137. The fix is to end the script with exec python train.py so python becomes PID 1. Running under tini or docker --init also reaps orphaned data-loader workers.
strong_answer_contains: Names PID 1 as the only signal receiver
Gives the exec fix and mentions an init process
questions.weak_answer: Says to raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which only delays the kill.
questions.follow_up: How would the same job save a checkpoint when it does receive SIGTERM?

questions.question: Why must memlock and nofile limits be raised on a GPU compute node, and why does editing limits.conf not fix a systemd service?
questions.model_answer: RDMA and CUDA pinned host memory lock large buffers in RAM, so the node needs memlock unlimited. Distributed training opens many sockets and shard files, so it needs a high nofile value. PAM applies /etc/security/limits.conf only to login sessions. A systemd service ignores that file, so the unit file needs LimitMEMLOCK=infinity and LimitNOFILE.
strong_answer_contains: Links memlock to RDMA and pinned memory
Knows PAM applies limits.conf only to logins
Puts the fix in the unit file
questions.weak_answer: Says to run ulimit -n in the shell before starting the service and does not know why it fails under systemd.
questions.follow_up: How do you check the limits a running process really has?

questions.question: Service A needs service B. You wrote Requires=B.service and A still starts before B is ready. Why?
questions.model_answer: Requires= and Wants= say only what must be started. Ordering is a separate setting. Without After=B.service, systemd starts both units at the same moment. You need the dependency line and the ordering line together.
strong_answer_contains: Names After= or Before= as the ordering keys
Notes the two lines are usually written as a pair
questions.weak_answer: Believes Requires= implies start order.
questions.follow_up: What changes if B only starts a socket and the real daemon comes later?

questions.question: How do you stop a runaway GPU job from taking sshd and kubelet down with it, and why must MemoryMax never be set on system.slice?
questions.model_answer: system.slice holds sshd, kubelet, containerd, slurmd and journald. A MemoryMax there makes the kernel throttle or kill the very daemons you need to recover the node. Protect them with a CPU weight and a memory low setting on system.slice and a strongly negative OOMScoreAdjust on sshd and kubelet. Enforce hard memory limits on the job slices, not on the system slice.
strong_answer_contains: Uses protection settings, not a hard cap, on system.slice
Puts the hard limit on the job side
questions.weak_answer: Sets a large MemoryMax on system.slice to be safe.
questions.follow_up: How would you confirm after the change that the OOM killer picks the job first?

questions.question: A data-loader runs on socket 0 and feeds a GPU on socket 1. What is the first-touch rule and how does it hurt here?
questions.model_answer: Under the default local policy a page is placed on the NUMA node of the core that first writes it. A loader on socket 0 faults its batch buffers there, so every host-to-device copy crosses the link between sockets. The fix is to start each rank bound to the NUMA node of its GPU, using numactl with both cpunodebind and membind.
strong_answer_contains: Binds both CPU and memory to the GPU's node
questions.weak_answer: Says to add more loader workers.
questions.follow_up: How do you find which NUMA node a GPU belongs to?

questions.question: What is the recommended Transparent Huge Pages policy for training nodes versus latency-sensitive services, and why?
questions.model_answer: Explicit huge pages come from a reserved pool and applications opt in. Transparent Huge Pages back memory with 2 MiB pages automatically in always, madvise or never mode. Throughput-oriented training benefits from fewer TLB misses, so always or madvise suits it. Latency-sensitive services can suffer stalls from background compaction, so the chapter points to madvise or never for them. Check the actual default on your distribution before changing it.
strong_answer_contains: Ties the policy to the workload type
questions.weak_answer: Says THP should always be turned off.
questions.follow_up: What would you measure to prove THP caused a latency spike?

questions.question: Why does a forked PyTorch DataLoader use more and more RAM when the dataset is a Python list?
questions.model_answer: fork shares the parent's pages copy-on-write. Reading a Python object still writes its reference count, and that write copies the whole 4 KiB page into the worker. Over an epoch each worker copies most of the list. Store the data in NumPy arrays, Arrow tables or memory-mapped files, which have no per-item reference counts.
strong_answer_contains: Explains reference counts as hidden writes
Offers a layout without per-object counts
questions.weak_answer: Blames a memory leak in PyTorch.
questions.follow_up: How would you show the sharing is working using PSS rather than RSS?

questions.question: NIC and NVMe interrupts are slowing your GPU data loaders. How do you see it and how do you isolate it?
questions.model_answer: Interrupts and their softirqs preempt user threads on the core they are routed to. You see them as irq and soft time in mpstat per CPU and in /proc/interrupts. You steer them away by setting smp_affinity_list per IRQ or the irqaffinity boot parameter, and you stop irqbalance from moving them back.
strong_answer_contains: Names mpstat and /proc/interrupts as the evidence
Sets IRQ affinity to housekeeping cores
questions.weak_answer: Pins the training process to cores but leaves interrupts where they are.
questions.follow_up: Which cores would you keep as housekeeping on a two-socket node?

questions.question: Is there a container object in the Linux kernel? What actually makes a container?
questions.model_answer: No, there is no container object. A container is an ordinary process tree. Namespaces limit what it can see. Cgroups limit what it can use. A root filesystem gives it its own view of the file tree, and capabilities, seccomp and security modules limit what it can do. All of it runs on the one host kernel.
strong_answer_contains: Says there is no kernel container object
questions.weak_answer: Describes a container as a lightweight virtual machine.
questions.follow_up: What does that shared kernel mean for security between tenants?

questions.question: You delete a secret file in a later Dockerfile RUN step. Is the secret gone from the image?
questions.model_answer: No. OverlayFS records a delete as a whiteout in the upper layer, which only hides the name. The bytes stay in the earlier read-only layer, and anyone who pulls the image can read them. Keep secrets out of build layers, use build secrets or multi-stage builds, and rotate any secret that was baked in.
strong_answer_contains: Knows the lower layer keeps the bytes
Gives a build-time fix and says to rotate
questions.weak_answer: Says the file is deleted because it no longer appears in the container.
questions.follow_up: How would you find which layer contains the file?

questions.question: What must a container runtime do to give a container a GPU, and why must you never bake libcuda into the image?
questions.model_answer: It exposes the /dev/nvidia device nodes in the container, allows their major and minor numbers in the devices cgroup, and bind-mounts the host's user-space driver libraries and nvidia-smi. A libcuda baked into the image can disagree with the host kernel driver and fail with a version mismatch. Keeping the user-space driver on the host keeps the pair matched.
strong_answer_contains: Lists devices, cgroup allow and library mounts
Knows the container carries only the toolkit-level CUDA libraries
questions.weak_answer: Says the image should carry the full driver so it is portable.
questions.follow_up: What does CDI change about how this injection is described?

questions.question: How do you replace a critical metadata or checkpoint-index file so a crash never leaves it half written?
questions.model_answer: Write the new content to a temporary file in the same directory so it is on the same filesystem. Call fsync on that file. Rename it over the target name, which is atomic. Then call fsync on the parent directory so the rename itself is durable. A reader then sees either the old file or the new one, never a mix.
strong_answer_contains: Same directory for the temp file
Explains why the directory fsync matters
questions.weak_answer: Opens the target with truncate and writes in place.
questions.follow_up: Where does this pattern appear in checkpoint publishing for training?

questions.question: What are the two queues behind listen(), and how do you tell which one is overflowing?
questions.model_answer: The SYN queue holds half-open connections that wait for the final ACK. The accept queue holds finished connections that wait for the application to call accept. Its size is the smaller of the backlog argument and net.core.somaxconn. When the accept queue is full the kernel drops or refuses new connections, and the listen-overflow counters rise. Check ss on the listening socket and the TCP extended counters from nstat.
strong_answer_contains: Names both queues and their size knobs
Points to ss and nstat counters
Notes a slow accept loop is the usual cause
questions.weak_answer: Says to raise somaxconn without checking why the application is slow to accept.
questions.follow_up: What does tcp_syncookies change about the SYN queue?

questions.question: Contrast TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT. Which one points to a bug in your server?
questions.model_answer: The side that sends the first FIN enters TIME_WAIT after its final ACK and stays there for twice the maximum segment lifetime. That is normal protocol hygiene. The side that receives the FIN and has ACKed it enters CLOSE_WAIT and stays until its own application closes the socket. Many CLOSE_WAIT sockets mean the server code is not closing connections.
strong_answer_contains: Says which side enters each state
Calls a pile of CLOSE_WAIT an application bug
questions.weak_answer: Treats TIME_WAIT as the leak and tunes the kernel to shorten it.
questions.follow_up: When can many TIME_WAIT sockets still cause real trouble?

questions.question: An RPC call has a steady 40 ms delay. What is the likely cause and the fix?
questions.model_answer: Nagle's algorithm holds a small write while earlier data is unacknowledged. Delayed ACK holds the receiver's acknowledgement for up to about 40 ms. If the client writes a header and then a body, the body waits for the ACK of the header. The fix is to send the request in one write or set TCP_NODELAY on the socket.
strong_answer_contains: Names Nagle plus delayed ACK together
Recognises the round number as a timer
Gives a one-write or TCP_NODELAY fix
questions.weak_answer: Blames the network path and asks for a faster link.
questions.follow_up: How would you prove it from a packet capture?

questions.question: Define the bandwidth-delay product and use it to explain why one TCP stream over a long link is slow.
questions.model_answer: The bandwidth-delay product is bandwidth times round-trip time. It is the amount of data that must be in flight to keep the pipe full. At 10 Gb per second and 70 ms it is 87.5 MB. A single connection with a 4 MB window can send at most window divided by RTT, about 57 MB per second, which is far below the link rate. So you need window scaling, bigger buffers or several streams.
strong_answer_contains: Names window size as the limiter
questions.weak_answer: Says TCP is slow over distance without a reason.
questions.follow_up: Which sysctls bound the receive window on Linux?

questions.question: Why do external DNS lookups from a Kubernetes pod feel slow and load CoreDNS heavily?
questions.model_answer: Pods get ndots:5 so short in-cluster names match the search list. An external name with fewer than five dots is tried with each search suffix first, and each try is a failed query. One lookup becomes several. Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot, lower ndots for the pod, or run a node-local DNS cache.
strong_answer_contains: Explains ndots and the search list
Offers FQDN, ndots or node-local cache
questions.weak_answer: Says CoreDNS needs more replicas and stops there.
questions.follow_up: How would you see the extra queries in a capture?

questions.question: Pods see random 5-second DNS delays. What is the cause and what fixes it?
questions.model_answer: A pod sends the A and AAAA queries in parallel from one socket, so both share the same five-tuple. Both go to the cluster DNS Service address and race in the connection-tracking NAT table. One packet is dropped, and the resolver waits five seconds before it retries. A node-local DNS cache avoids the Service NAT path for those queries.
strong_answer_contains: Names the parallel A and AAAA queries
Gives node-local cache as the fix
questions.weak_answer: Says DNS is unreliable and adds retries.
questions.follow_up: What counter would show the conntrack insert failures?

questions.question: 500 GPU nodes pull images through one NAT gateway and new connections fail. What happened?
questions.model_answer: A single public address has only about sixty thousand source ports for each remote address and port. Hundreds of parallel streams from 500 nodes to one registry address use them up, and sockets in TIME_WAIT make it worse. Fixes are more NAT addresses, a regional registry mirror or cache inside the network, and fewer parallel pulls.
strong_answer_contains: Links it to the registry fan-in
Gives address, cache and pull-limit fixes
questions.weak_answer: Says the registry is slow.
questions.follow_up: How would a cluster-wide image-pull stampede be avoided at start of a job?

questions.question: Why must NAT never sit inside an InfiniBand or RoCE v2 training fabric?
questions.model_answer: During queue-pair setup the ranks exchange addresses and queue-pair numbers and program them into the network card. A middlebox that rewrites addresses or ports in flight makes that state wrong. It also breaks hardware offload and adds a stateful bottleneck. The back-end fabric should be routed, not translated.
strong_answer_contains: Explains addresses are programmed into hardware
States routed fabric as the design
questions.weak_answer: Says NAT is fine if the table is large.
questions.follow_up: Where does NAT belong in an AI cluster instead?

questions.question: Why does a layer 4 load balancer spread gRPC traffic badly, and how do you fix it?
questions.model_answer: gRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. A layer 4 balancer chooses a backend once, at connection setup. All the calls from that client then go to one backend. Fix it with a layer 7 proxy that balances per call, client-side balancing, or connection limits that force regular reconnects.
strong_answer_contains: Says the choice is made once
questions.weak_answer: Suggests round robin on connections as the fix.
questions.follow_up: What changes for long streaming token responses?

questions.question: Why is active connection count a poor load signal for LLM backends, and what should the router use?
questions.model_answer: A 32,000-token prompt uses far more compute and cache memory than a 50-token prompt, yet both count as one request. A router should look at queue depth, cache usage and, where supported, prefix-cache match. Weighted by actual work, it avoids sending heavy requests to a saturated backend.
strong_answer_contains: Shows one request is not one unit of work
questions.weak_answer: Uses least connections and adds replicas.
questions.follow_up: How would you stop prefix-cache routing from overloading one pod?

questions.question: Packets are being lost on a Linux host. How do you tell a link problem from a ring-buffer, backlog or socket-buffer drop?
questions.model_answer: Link errors show as CRC and frame errors in ethtool statistics and in ip -s link. Ring-buffer exhaustion shows as missed or no-buffer counters in the same ethtool output. Backlog drops show in the softnet statistics. Socket-buffer drops show in the protocol counters and in ss. Each layer has its own counter, so you read them in order from the wire upward.
questions.weak_answer: Runs ping and concludes the network is fine.
questions.follow_up: Which of these would point at a bad optic?

questions.question: A stall lasts exactly 5 seconds, or exactly 60. What do you suspect first?
questions.model_answer: Hardware faults do not keep to round durations. A round time is a software or protocol timer. About 40 ms suggests delayed ACK with Nagle. 200 ms matches the minimum retransmission timeout. One, three or seven seconds match SYN retransmission backoff, which hints at a full accept queue or a drop. Five seconds fits the DNS retry. Match the number to the timer.
questions.weak_answer: Starts replacing cables.
questions.follow_up: Which timer fits a stall of about one minute?

questions.question: What makes an operational script such as a node-drain tool safe to run at 3 a.m.?
questions.model_answer: It is idempotent, so running it again on a node that is already drained changes nothing. It has a dry-run mode that prints each destructive command without running it. It isolates errors per item and stops after a failure budget. It logs what it did and exits with a clear status code. These properties let a tired engineer run it without fear.
strong_answer_contains: Per-item error isolation with a failure budget
questions.weak_answer: Says it is safe because it was tested once.
questions.follow_up: How would you test the dry-run path without a cluster?

questions.question: Why pass subprocess.run an argument list instead of shell=True, and what do check, timeout and stdin do?
questions.model_answer: A list calls the program directly with no shell, so a hostname containing a semicolon or a command substitution stays a plain string. check=True raises an error on a non-zero exit. timeout stops a hung child from blocking the script. Closing stdin stops a child from waiting on a prompt that no one can answer.
questions.weak_answer: Uses shell=True for convenience and quotes the input by hand.
questions.follow_up: What goes wrong with a pipe deadlock on Popen?

questions.question: A script submits ten million tasks to a thread pool and runs out of memory. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.model_answer: Submitting everything first creates ten million future objects and queue entries before the workers drain any. The fix is bounded submission. Seed the pool with a limited number of in-flight futures and add one new task each time one finishes. Memory then depends on the window, not on the input size.
strong_answer_contains: Mentions memory depends on the window
questions.weak_answer: Adds more workers.
questions.follow_up: How would you apply the same bound in asyncio?

questions.question: 1,000 clients retry a recovering service on a fixed schedule and keep knocking it over. What do you change?
questions.model_answer: Fixed retry times line the clients up, so each wave hits the server at the same instant. Use exponential backoff with full jitter. Each client waits a random time between zero and a growing cap. The retries spread out, and the server can recover. Add a retry budget so total retries stay bounded.
strong_answer_contains: Adds a cap or retry budget
questions.weak_answer: Shortens the retry interval so clients recover faster.
questions.follow_up: Where else in a platform does the same herd effect show up?

questions.question: Why prefer a fake with dependency injection over heavy mock patching when testing cluster tools?
questions.model_answer: A fake is a small working in-memory version of the dependency. The tool receives it through its constructor, so the test exercises real logic and checks the outcome. Patching ties tests to how the code looks up names and breaks when the code is refactored. Fakes also let you simulate failures such as a node that will not drain.
strong_answer_contains: Defines stub, fake, spy and mock
questions.weak_answer: Mocks every call and asserts they were made in order.
questions.follow_up: How do you test code that reads /proc or /sys on a laptop?

questions.question: Why must a Terraform pipeline apply the exact plan file that was reviewed?
questions.model_answer: If the pipeline plans for review and then runs a new apply after the merge, anything that changed in between is applied unreviewed. That could be a change in state, in the cloud, or in a data source. Saving the plan with the out option and applying that file means the reviewed change is the applied change. A stale plan is refused.
strong_answer_contains: Names the gap between plan and apply
Notes a stale plan is rejected
questions.weak_answer: Says apply with auto-approve is fine because tests passed.
questions.follow_up: How do you keep two pipelines from applying at once?

questions.question: What makes an Ansible task idempotent, and what breaks it?
questions.model_answer: A task is idempotent when a second run on a host already in the right state changes nothing and reports ok. A template that embeds a timestamp or random value renders a different file every run, so the task always reports changed and restarts services. Use modules with state, and use creates, changed_when and checks for commands.
strong_answer_contains: Defines changed equals zero on re-run
questions.weak_answer: Says idempotent means the playbook can be run twice without errors.
questions.follow_up: How does check mode help prove idempotency?

questions.question: How do you roll an Ansible change across 1,000 GPU nodes safely?
questions.model_answer: Use serial with growing batches, for example one host, then ten percent, then all. The first host is a canary. Set a maximum failure percentage so a bad change stops early. Run a health check after each batch before moving on. Keep the change reversible and the inventory split so you can pause.
questions.weak_answer: Runs the playbook on all nodes at once with a high fork count.
questions.follow_up: How would you add a rollback step?

questions.question: Why must secret-handling tasks set both no_log and diff off?
questions.model_answer: no_log hides the task arguments and result from the normal output, verbose output and callback logs. Diff mode can still print the before and after content of a file or template. A task that writes a secret into a file would leak it through the diff. Set both, and avoid passing secrets on command lines.
questions.weak_answer: Sets no_log only.
questions.follow_up: How would you debug such a task without leaking the secret?

questions.question: Someone deleted the Terraform state file from the bucket. What do you do?
questions.model_answer: If the bucket has versioning, list the object versions and restore the version just before the current one. Then run a plan, which should show no changes. Without versioning you must rebuild the state by importing resources, which is slow and risky. That is why state buckets need versioning, locking and restricted access.
strong_answer_contains: Notes the import fallback and prevention
questions.weak_answer: Re-runs apply and lets Terraform recreate everything.
questions.follow_up: Why must state never be stored in Git?

questions.question: You need a quick kubectl hotfix but GitOps self-heal is on. What happens and what is the right procedure?
questions.model_answer: Self-heal overwrites a manual edit within seconds. In an emergency you first pause automatic sync for that application, then apply the hotfix and verify it. Afterward you put the same change into Git and resume sync. Record the break-glass action so the audit trail is complete.
strong_answer_contains: Commits the fix back to Git
questions.weak_answer: Disables the GitOps controller for the whole cluster and forgets to turn it back on.
questions.follow_up: How do you handle an HPA that makes Argo show out of sync?

questions.question: Why must the RDMA driver stack go in before the GPU driver and the peer-memory module on a node?
questions.model_answer: The peer-memory module registers GPU memory pages with the RDMA core using symbols from the matching network driver. If the GPU driver is built before the right OFED or DOCA stack is present, the module is missing or built against the wrong symbols. GPUDirect RDMA then silently falls back to a slower path. Order the roles and verify the module loads.
questions.weak_answer: Installs in any order and reboots until it works.
questions.follow_up: How would Ansible verify GPUDirect RDMA is active after the roles run?

questions.question: An upgrade playbook hangs forever on 256 GPU nodes. What are the usual causes?
questions.model_answer: The package manager can stop at a prompt about a modified configuration file with no terminal attached. It can also wait on a lock held by an automatic update service. Use non-interactive settings, keep the old config option, wait for the lock with a timeout, disable automatic updates during the window, and set a task timeout.
questions.weak_answer: Re-runs the playbook until it passes.
questions.follow_up: What stops automatic kernel updates from breaking DKMS modules?

questions.question: The API server and etcd go down during a multi-node training run. What happens to the running pods?
questions.model_answer: Running pods keep running. The containers are managed locally by the container runtime and the kubelet, and the network rules stay programmed in the node kernels. So the training job continues. What stops is anything that needs the API: new pods, scaling, rescheduling and status updates. A node that fails during the outage cannot be replaced until the control plane returns.
strong_answer_contains: Separates running state from control actions
Names the kubelet and runtime as local owners
Says what cannot happen during the outage
questions.weak_answer: Says all pods are killed because the control plane is gone.
questions.follow_up: What happens when the kubelet stops heartbeating but the API is healthy?

questions.question: Trace the timeline when a worker node stops heartbeating.
questions.model_answer: The kubelet renews a lease about every ten seconds. After the node-monitor grace period, which defaults to forty seconds, the node lifecycle controller marks the node unknown and adds taints. Pods then become eligible for eviction after their toleration time. Only then are replacements scheduled. A stateful or gang job may need extra steps, so recovery is slower than people expect.
strong_answer_contains: Names the lease and grace period
questions.weak_answer: Says pods move at once when a node dies.
questions.follow_up: How would you make GPU job recovery faster and still safe?

questions.question: etcd reports a no-space alarm and every write fails. What is going on and how do you recover?
questions.model_answer: When the database reaches its size quota, etcd raises an alarm and the cluster becomes read-only. Writes fail with a database-space-exceeded error. Compact old revisions, defragment each member, then disarm the alarm. Find what filled the database, such as an event storm or a controller writing in a loop.
questions.weak_answer: Raises the quota and moves on.
questions.follow_up: Why do large clusters keep events in a separate etcd?

questions.question: You restore etcd from a snapshot taken two hours ago. What is lost and what surprises do you get?
questions.model_answer: The restore rewinds desired state to the snapshot time. Anything created in the last two hours disappears from the API. Kubelets then find running pods the API does not know and may delete them. Objects deleted since the snapshot come back. Plan the restore with all control-plane components stopped and tell users what window is lost.
questions.weak_answer: Says a restore is harmless because the data is backed up.
questions.follow_up: Which files besides the snapshot do you need for a full control-plane recovery?

questions.question: A node-health controller finds 80 percent of nodes unhealthy at once. Why must it have a concurrency budget?
questions.model_answer: A bad configuration, a faulty exporter upgrade or a power event can raise the same alert on most nodes together. Without a limit the controller would cordon and drain most of the cluster and turn a monitoring fault into an outage. A cap on concurrent actions and a pause when too many nodes are bad limits the blast radius.
strong_answer_contains: Adds a pause or escalation for mass failure
questions.weak_answer: Says the controller should act on every unhealthy node immediately.
questions.follow_up: What signal separates a real fleet fault from a bad alert?

questions.question: How does the kubelet decide memory pressure, and why is that not the same as free in meminfo?
questions.model_answer: Free memory is mostly used for page cache, so MemFree is near zero on a busy node even when plenty is reclaimable. The kubelet reads the cgroup memory statistics and subtracts the inactive file cache from usage to compute an available figure. Eviction thresholds apply to that number. Look at that number, not at free.
strong_answer_contains: Says to watch available, not free
questions.weak_answer: Alerts on low MemFree.
questions.follow_up: In what order does the kubelet pick pods to evict?

questions.question: A container with a CPU limit fails its liveness probe even though the application is fine. Why?
questions.model_answer: A strict CPU quota throttles every thread in the container for the rest of the period during a burst. The probe handler is throttled too and times out. The throttle counters in cpu.stat rise. The fix is a more generous or no CPU limit, a longer probe timeout, or a startup probe. Do not treat the probe failure as an application bug.
strong_answer_contains: Links the quota to the probe timeout
questions.weak_answer: Restarts the pod and hopes.
questions.follow_up: Why do GPU pods often run without CPU limits?

questions.question: A gRPC client sends 10,000 requests through a ClusterIP Service and one vLLM pod gets all of them. Why?
questions.model_answer: Service balancing works per TCP connection at layer 4. The backend is chosen once at connect time, and every call on that long-lived HTTP/2 connection follows it. Use a headless Service with client-side balancing, a layer 7 proxy or an inference-aware gateway, and limit connection age so clients reconnect.
strong_answer_contains: Gives a layer 7 or client-side fix
questions.weak_answer: Adds more replicas.
questions.follow_up: How does a prefix-aware router change this?

questions.question: The scheduler says 20 nodes have insufficient GPU, but Grafana shows many of them idle. Why?
questions.model_answer: The scheduler works from resource requests compared with node allocatable, never from live utilisation. An idle notebook or a stuck job can hold GPU requests without using them. Look at what holds the allocations on each node. Then reclaim them or add quota and idle-timeout policies.
strong_answer_contains: Finds the holder of the allocation
questions.weak_answer: Says the scheduler is broken or the metrics are wrong.
questions.follow_up: Which event text distinguishes a capacity shortage from an affinity mismatch?

questions.question: Two 4-pod training jobs are submitted to a cluster with 6 free nodes. What deadlock can occur and how do you avoid it?
questions.model_answer: The default scheduler places pods one at a time. Three pods of each job may land on the six nodes. Each job waits for its fourth rank and holds its nodes, so neither can start. This is hold and wait. A queueing layer or gang scheduler admits a job only when all its pods can be placed.
questions.weak_answer: Says the cluster simply needs more nodes.
questions.follow_up: How does Kueue prevent this without replacing the scheduler?

questions.question: All kubeadm certificates expired because the cluster was not upgraded for 13 months. What happens and how do you recover?
questions.model_answer: Kubectl and the kubelet fail with certificate-expired errors, and the control-plane parts cannot talk to each other. Running containers keep running. Renew the certificates with kubeadm, restart the control-plane static pods and refresh the kubeconfig files. Then add expiry monitoring and a calendar so it does not repeat.
strong_answer_contains: Adds monitoring to prevent a repeat
questions.weak_answer: Rebuilds the cluster.
questions.follow_up: What else expires on a similar clock?

questions.question: Why is raw GPU utilisation a poor autoscaling signal for LLM serving, and what do you scale on instead?
questions.model_answer: The utilisation metric shows the share of time at least one kernel ran. A single request keeps the GPU busy about as much as a full batch. It does not tell you queue pressure. Scale on queue depth or time in queue, cache usage and latency measures from the server, and combine with a slow-start-aware policy.
strong_answer_contains: Explains what the metric really measures
questions.weak_answer: Scales at 80 percent GPU utilisation.
questions.follow_up: How do you stop the autoscaler overshooting while pods load weights?

questions.question: Pod A cannot reach Service B. Describe a bisection.
questions.model_answer: Test in hops from the client pod. First a backend pod on the same node by pod IP. Then a backend on another node by pod IP. Then the Service by cluster IP. Then the Service by DNS name. The first hop that fails tells you the layer: application, pod network, service rules or DNS. Capture in the right network namespace to confirm.
strong_answer_contains: Uses nsenter or similar for capture
questions.weak_answer: Restarts kube-proxy first.
questions.follow_up: How do you check conntrack exhaustion on the node?

questions.question: A multi-node job hangs right after NCCL prints its bootstrap interface. How do you debug?
questions.model_answer: The bootstrap ring uses the socket interface and then the ranks exchange fabric information. A hang here usually means a wrong interface, a blocked port, a missing device or an unreachable peer. Check NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, run with NCCL debug output, test reachability between pods and check the RDMA devices are visible in the pod.
questions.weak_answer: Reboots the nodes.
questions.follow_up: Which volume setting do multi-GPU pods often need?

questions.question: Why is create on pods almost the same as read access to secrets in a namespace?
questions.model_answer: A user who can create a pod can mount any secret in that namespace as a volume, or run the pod under a powerful service account, and then print the contents. So pod-creation rights reach the secrets. Limit who can create pods, enforce admission policy and separate sensitive namespaces.
strong_answer_contains: Explains the mount and service-account path
Calls it privilege escalation by design
Names admission policy as the control
questions.weak_answer: Says secrets are protected by a separate permission.
questions.follow_up: How does Pod Security Admission limit what such a pod can do?

questions.question: A 13B model in FP16 sits on an 80 GB H100. What is the lower bound on decode latency per token at batch one?
questions.model_answer: The weights take 13 billion times two bytes, which is 26 GB. At batch one every token reads all the weights once. With 3,350 GB per second of memory bandwidth the floor is about 7.76 ms per token. The free memory does not lower this floor. Only more bandwidth, smaller weights or larger batches do.
strong_answer_contains: Says spare memory does not help
questions.weak_answer: Quotes the compute rate in FLOPS as the limit.
questions.follow_up: How does batching change the picture?

questions.question: Four L40S GPUs run a 70B model with tensor parallelism and latency is bad despite strong FP8 compute. Why?
questions.model_answer: The L40S has no NVLink. Tensor parallelism runs an all-reduce on every layer, so every step crosses the PCIe bus. The Tensor Cores wait for data. Use NVLink-connected GPUs for tensor parallelism, or reduce the parallel degree.
questions.weak_answer: Says FP8 should have made it fast.
questions.follow_up: How do you read nvidia-smi topo -m to check this on a node?

questions.question: topo -m shows NV18 for every pair, yet one pair has a third of the expected bandwidth. How do you find out why?
questions.model_answer: The topology command shows static discovery only. A link can be down or noisy. Check nvlink status for a dead sub-link and the error counters for replay and CRC errors, and run a point-to-point bandwidth test per pair. A failing link points to hardware service.
strong_answer_contains: Names nvlink status and error counters
questions.weak_answer: Reboots the node and retests.
questions.follow_up: What would the NCCL result look like on that node?

questions.question: Why can nvidia-smi show 100 percent utilisation while the GPU does almost no useful math?
questions.model_answer: The metric says that at least one kernel was running during the sample period. One warp spinning on one multiprocessor counts. The tensor cores can be idle. Use SM activity and tensor-core activity from DCGM, and throughput of the job itself.
questions.weak_answer: Treats 100 percent as healthy.
questions.follow_up: How do you tell compute-bound, memory-bound and stalled apart?

questions.question: What does persistence mode do, and what happens without it?
questions.model_answer: With no process holding the device open the driver can tear down its state. The next job waits for device initialisation, and power or clock settings reset. Persistence mode, normally via the persistence daemon, keeps the state loaded and removes that start-up stall.
questions.weak_answer: Says it is only a power saving feature.
questions.follow_up: Where would you enable it in a node bring-up playbook?

questions.question: Explain how you would use DCGM, Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute together on a slow job.
questions.model_answer: Use them in layers. DCGM and nvidia-smi give always-on telemetry and tell you something is wrong. Nsight Systems gives a timeline across CPU, I/O, copies and GPU streams and shows where gaps are. Nsight Compute inspects one kernel at a time. Go from the cheap broad view to the expensive narrow view only as needed.
questions.weak_answer: Starts with Nsight Compute on the whole job.
questions.follow_up: What overhead should you expect from each?

questions.question: Contrast a single-bit and a double-bit ECC error, and volatile and aggregate counters.
questions.model_answer: A single-bit error is corrected by hardware and the job continues. A double-bit error cannot be corrected, raises a serious Xid and halts the work. Volatile counters reset on a GPU reset or reboot. Aggregate counters persist over the life of the device. Trend the corrected errors, because a rising rate suggests a failing part.
questions.weak_answer: Says any ECC error means replace the GPU.
questions.follow_up: How does row remapping change the response on newer GPUs?

questions.question: What is the difference between Xid 63 and Xid 64?
questions.model_answer: Xid 63 is informational. It records a normal page retirement or row remap after a correctable event. Xid 64 is a failure of that mechanism, for example when spare rows run out. That is a hardware fault, so cordon the node and start a replacement. Triage Xids in tiers so you do not page for informational ones.
questions.weak_answer: Treats all Xids the same.
questions.follow_up: Which Xid tier drains a node automatically?

questions.question: After an Xid 79 you want to recover the GPU without rebooting the host. What are the steps and the gate?
questions.model_answer: Cordon and drain the node first. Remove the PCIe device and rescan the bus through sysfs. Confirm the GPU comes back at full link width and speed. Reload the driver if needed. Only a passing level-three diagnostic from DCGM lets you uncordon. If it fails, the node goes to hardware repair.
questions.weak_answer: Resets the GPU under a running job.
questions.follow_up: Why check link width after recovery?

questions.question: Kubernetes GPU pods work but Slurm container jobs report no devices after an image update. Why?
questions.model_answer: Kubernetes uses the container toolkit or CDI path. Slurm with Enroot and Pyxis relies on hook scripts that bind-mount the driver libraries and devices. If the hook file is missing after the image change, the GPU variables are unset inside the container. Compare the hook directory and the environment on a good node and a bad node.
questions.weak_answer: Reinstalls the driver.
questions.follow_up: What other node-image changes silently break GPU access?

questions.question: Clocks swing between 1,980 and 800 MHz at 65 C with no throttle reason. What is happening?
questions.model_answer: Short idle gaps between data-loader batches let firmware drop to lower power states. The clock then has to ramp up again. Enable persistence mode, set the CPU governor to performance and consider locking clocks. The better fix is also to remove the gaps by feeding data faster.
questions.weak_answer: Blames thermal throttling.
questions.follow_up: What does a throttle-reason bitmask tell you?

questions.question: Compute theoretical occupancy for 256-thread blocks at 40 and at 56 registers per thread on a 65,536-register multiprocessor.
questions.model_answer: At 40 registers the file holds 1,638 threads, which is six whole blocks or 48 warps, so 75 percent. At 56 registers it holds 1,170 threads, which is four whole blocks or 32 warps, so 50 percent. Only whole blocks count. More registers per thread cost occupancy.
questions.weak_answer: Ignores whole-block rounding.
questions.follow_up: What does the compiler flag for register and spill reporting show?

questions.question: Why does adding a RuntimeClass not make a GPU workload schedulable?
questions.model_answer: A RuntimeClass only tells the kubelet which runtime handler to use for the pod sandbox. It knows nothing about GPU inventory. A GPU becomes schedulable only after the device plugin advertises it as an extended resource on the node and the pod requests it.
strong_answer_contains: Names the device plugin as the source of inventory
questions.weak_answer: Says the runtime class gives the pod a GPU.
questions.follow_up: What do the toolkit and the plugin each do at pod start?

questions.question: Why enable the fail-on-init-error option on the device plugin in production?
questions.model_answer: If NVML fails to start, the plugin with that option on exits and crash-loops, which raises restart alerts at once. With it off, the container stays running and silently reports zero GPUs. The node then looks healthy while it cannot serve GPU pods. A loud failure is better.
questions.weak_answer: Leaves it off to avoid restarts.
questions.follow_up: How would you alert on a node with GPUs present but zero allocatable?

questions.question: A pod fails with an nvidia-container-cli mount error for a device file. At which stage did it fail?
questions.model_answer: It failed during runtime sandbox creation, before the entrypoint. Scheduling and device allocation had already succeeded. The runtime hook could not find or mount the device node on the host. Look at the driver state and device files on that node, not at the scheduler.
strong_answer_contains: Looks at the node, not the scheduler
questions.weak_answer: Says the scheduler picked a bad node.
questions.follow_up: Which tool shows what the runtime injected into the container?

questions.question: Why can a single pod never span two nodes, and what do you use for a 16-GPU job on 8-GPU nodes?
questions.model_answer: A pod is bound to one node and its containers share that node's kernel resources. A pod asking for more GPUs than one node has stays pending. A multi-node job is several pods, one or more per node, that coordinate through the application, for example through a distributed training framework over the fast network.
questions.weak_answer: Says Kubernetes will spread the pod.
questions.follow_up: What does rendezvous do in such a job?

questions.question: Two 8-node jobs share a 12-node cluster without gang scheduling. What can happen?
questions.model_answer: Pods of both jobs are placed as capacity appears, say six nodes each. Both jobs wait for the two missing nodes and neither starts, while all the GPUs sit allocated and idle. Gang scheduling or queued admission means a job starts only when all its pods fit.
questions.weak_answer: Calls it a rare bug.
questions.follow_up: How does Kueue admit a whole job?

questions.question: Why does a plain ResourceQuota waste GPUs, and how do Kueue cohorts help?
questions.model_answer: A ResourceQuota is a hard static ceiling per namespace. A team at its cap cannot use GPUs that other teams leave idle. Kueue cohorts let queues borrow unused quota from each other and reclaim it when the owner needs it back, so the cluster stays busy and each team keeps its guaranteed share.
questions.weak_answer: Raises the quota for everyone.
questions.follow_up: What does preemption do when a lender wants capacity back?

questions.question: What does BestEffortFIFO do when the head job cannot fit?
questions.model_answer: Strict FIFO blocks every job behind the head job, even small ones that would fit. Best-effort FIFO keeps the large job queued and admits smaller jobs that fit now. It improves utilisation, at the risk of starving the large job, so teams add backfill rules or priorities.
questions.weak_answer: Says it is the same as strict FIFO.
questions.follow_up: How do you stop starvation of large jobs?

questions.question: What limits of the device plugin model led to Dynamic Resource Allocation?
questions.model_answer: The plugin exposes integer counts, so a request cannot say which model, memory size or MIG state it wants. The scheduler cannot see how devices relate, for example a GPU and a NIC on the same PCIe switch. Allocation is static per container. DRA adds device classes and claims with attributes and selectors. Check the feature status for your Kubernetes version before relying on it.
questions.weak_answer: Says DRA replaces the plugin everywhere already.
questions.follow_up: How does a ResourceClaim differ from a limit on nvidia.com/gpu?

questions.question: What is the difference between a GPU instance and a compute instance in MIG?
questions.model_answer: A GPU instance is the hardware partition that isolates memory, memory controllers and cache slices. A compute instance sits inside a GPU instance and allocates some of its multiprocessors. Several compute instances in one GPU instance share that instance's memory.
strong_answer_contains: Memory isolation lives in the GI
questions.weak_answer: Treats them as the same thing.
questions.follow_up: What stays shared across all MIG slices on a card?

questions.question: A 7 GB model failed on a 1g.10gb MIG slice under load. Why, and what do you do?
questions.model_answer: Weights, cold start and steady state fit, but many concurrent sequences with long context push peak memory over ten gigabytes. The hardware wall is hard, so the process runs out of memory. Size the slice for peak, including cache, or pick a larger profile, and test at production concurrency.
strong_answer_contains: Includes cache growth in the sizing
questions.weak_answer: Sizes the slice from weight size alone.
questions.follow_up: Why is aggregate free GPU memory a bad capacity metric on a MIG cluster?

questions.question: Ten pods share one 16 GB GPU by time-slicing and one pod leaks memory. Why do the cgroups not protect the others?
questions.model_answer: Memory cgroups track host RAM, not memory inside the GPU. All pods see the same device and draw from the same pool. Time-slicing shares time but gives no memory isolation, so one leak can crash the others. Use MIG or MPS limits where isolation matters, or limit tenants to trusted workloads.
questions.weak_answer: Says set a memory limit on each pod.
questions.follow_up: How does MPS differ from time-slicing?

questions.question: Walk through how you pick a GPU sharing model.
questions.model_answer: Start with whether you need a virtual machine boundary, which points to vGPU. Next ask whether you need hardware-enforced memory and compute isolation, which points to MIG. Then ask whether workloads are trusted and cooperative, which allows MPS or time-slicing. Otherwise give whole GPUs. Offer few classes in the catalogue.
strong_answer_contains: Maps each answer to a model
questions.weak_answer: Picks time-slicing because it gives the most replicas.
questions.follow_up: What goes wrong when a workload moves from time-sliced to MIG?

questions.question: Why does one dropped packet hurt a 400 Gbps RoCEv2 link so much?
questions.model_answer: At that speed and a round trip of about twenty microseconds, roughly 250 packets are in flight. With go-back-n recovery the receiver discards every packet after the lost one and the sender repeats them all. Selective repeat would resend only the lost packet. That is why RoCE fabrics aim to be lossless and why loss shows up as a large throughput drop.
questions.weak_answer: Says a single drop costs one packet.
questions.follow_up: What does PFC do to keep the fabric lossless, and what can go wrong?

questions.question: Throughput is low, drops are zero. Which counters show congestion control is throttling the job?
questions.model_answer: Read per-second changes in the ECN-marked, congestion-event and PFC counters on the switch and the NIC, and the RDMA counters for congestion notifications handled. Zero drops with these rising means DCQCN and PFC are slowing the sender. Compare deltas, not totals.
questions.weak_answer: Concludes the network is healthy because nothing is dropped.
questions.follow_up: What would a healthy DCQCN loop look like in the counters?

questions.question: Why must the DCQCN thresholds be ordered XON below K-min below K-max below XOFF below the buffer size?
questions.model_answer: ECN marking has to start early and reach its maximum before the buffer reaches the PFC pause threshold. That gives the sender time to slow down before a pause frame is needed. The pause threshold must sit below the buffer limit to preserve losslessness. If the order is wrong, PFC fires first and spreads pauses.
questions.weak_answer: Sets ECN thresholds higher than the pause threshold.
questions.follow_up: What is a PFC storm and how does the watchdog help?

questions.question: On a leaf switch one port shows heavy transmitted and received pause frames and a full queue, while another shows many ECN marks and no transmitted pauses. Where is the bottleneck?
questions.model_answer: The first port is a middle hop. It receives pause from downstream and passes it upstream. The second port sits nearest the receiver and shows congestion at the edge. The fix belongs at the receiver-side bottleneck, such as incast to one host, not at the middle hop.
questions.weak_answer: Tunes the busiest-looking port.
questions.follow_up: How would you confirm incast from the application side?

questions.question: SSH sessions stall during training bursts. The QoS output shows PFC on priorities 0 and 3. What is wrong?
questions.model_answer: PFC is on priority 0, which carries default traffic such as management. Backpressure from training can pause it. Enable PFC only on the RoCE priority. Re-run a congestion test and confirm pause counters on priority 0 stay at zero.
strong_answer_contains: Limits PFC to the RoCE class
questions.weak_answer: Raises the SSH timeout.
questions.follow_up: Which DSCP and class settings does the chapter give as lossless RoCE defaults?

questions.question: Why does standard RoCEv2 balance badly across equal-cost paths in AI training?
questions.model_answer: Traffic between rail-aligned GPUs uses few distinct addresses, and every frame has the same UDP destination port. A small number of long-lived flows have the same hash inputs, so they land on the same links. That is low entropy. Remedies include dynamic or per-packet load balancing, more queue pairs and careful source-port use.
questions.weak_answer: Says ECMP always spreads load evenly.
questions.follow_up: How does adaptive routing on InfiniBand differ?

questions.question: A 400 Gbps port reports link up, yet the host sees about 16 GB per second. Why?
questions.model_answer: The PCIe link may have trained down, for example to a narrower width, because of riser wiring or bifurcation. The slot then caps DMA throughput regardless of the network speed. lspci shows the link capability next to the link status. Reseat or fix the slot and retrain.
strong_answer_contains: Network speed is not host speed
questions.weak_answer: Blames the switch.
questions.follow_up: How does this show up in an nccl-tests result?

questions.question: Why is AllReduce equal to ReduceScatter followed by AllGather, and who uses this?
questions.model_answer: ReduceScatter leaves each rank with its reduced shard of the data. AllGather then circulates the shards so every rank has the full result. Fully sharded data parallel uses the two halves separately: it gathers parameters before use and reduces-scatters gradients after the backward pass.
strong_answer_contains: Each rank holds one shard in the middle
questions.weak_answer: Calls them unrelated operations.
questions.follow_up: Which has more bytes on the wire per rank in a ring?

questions.question: Why bind ranks to NUMA nodes and set NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY?
questions.model_answer: A launcher or taskset that pins a rank to a narrow CPU mask is inherited by NCCL's helper threads. They can collapse onto one core and slow the network path. Bind each rank to the NUMA domain of its GPU, and tell NCCL to ignore the inherited affinity so its threads spread across that domain.
questions.weak_answer: Pins each rank to a single core for stability.
questions.follow_up: How do you check the GPU-to-NUMA map?

questions.question: An NCCL timeout is logged by a healthy rank. Why is it the wrong rank to blame?
questions.model_answer: Collectives act as barriers. Healthy ranks finish their work, enter the collective first and start their watchdog timers. They time out while waiting for the slow or dead rank. So the first log line points at a waiting rank. Find which rank is behind using flight-recorder data or the NCCL RAS tool, then check that node.
strong_answer_contains: Finds the lagging rank with tools
questions.weak_answer: Replaces the node that logged the error.
questions.follow_up: What does a mismatch in operation counts tell you?

questions.question: NCCL fails with a system error about no space in /dev/shm in a container. Why, and how do you size it?
questions.model_answer: The default shared-memory size of 64 MiB is too small for an 8-GPU node, because NCCL places buffers there. The chapter's worked example needs over a gigabyte. Set a larger shared memory size for the pod, using a memory-backed volume, and check the NCCL buffer settings.
strong_answer_contains: Says shared memory carries NCCL buffers
questions.weak_answer: Increases the host disk.
questions.follow_up: Which memlock failure looks similar at start-up?

questions.question: Explain how GPUDirect RDMA works and what the peer-memory module does.
questions.model_answer: Without it, data from GPU memory is copied to host memory and then sent by the NIC. With it, the NIC reads GPU memory directly across PCIe. The peer-memory module registers GPU pages with the RDMA core so the NIC can address them. Freeing a registered buffer triggers invalidation, so memory registrations must be managed with care.
strong_answer_contains: Registers GPU pages with RDMA core
questions.weak_answer: Says it makes the network faster by itself.
questions.follow_up: How does PCIe ACS get in the way?

questions.question: In the 1.2 million image benchmark, where does the per-file time go, and what does that tell you about the fix?
questions.model_answer: The chapter's benchmark spends 4 ms per file on metadata and read syscalls and 15 ms on CPU decode and augmentation. So CPU work dominates in that case, and a faster file system alone would not fix it. Measure first, then decide between sharded formats for the metadata part and more workers or GPU decode for the CPU part.
strong_answer_contains: Splits time into storage and CPU
Matches fix to the dominant part
questions.weak_answer: Buys faster storage first.
questions.follow_up: How do you separate loader overhead from storage time experimentally?

questions.question: When random reads cannot be avoided, what do you change about read-ahead and I/O calls?
questions.model_answer: Large read-ahead wastes bandwidth on random reads and fills the page cache with blocks nobody uses. Turn it down. Use positional reads or batched asynchronous I/O with registered buffers and direct I/O to cut syscall cost and hide latency. Test on your data, because the right setting depends on the access pattern.
questions.weak_answer: Increases read-ahead for speed.
questions.follow_up: How do WebDataset style shards avoid random reads?

questions.question: Why is a sharded checkpoint write so much faster than gathering to rank 0?
questions.model_answer: Gathering moves the whole payload to one rank and writes it from one node. In the chapter's 70B example that takes about 269 seconds. A sharded write has each GPU write its own shard in parallel, so the time shrinks with the number of writers until the storage limit. It also avoids a memory spike on rank 0.
questions.weak_answer: Says compression is the main gain.
questions.follow_up: How does the load side handle a different GPU count?

questions.question: State Young's and Daly's formulas for checkpoint interval and say what the variables mean.
questions.model_answer: Young's interval is the square root of two times the write time times the cluster mean time between failures. Daly's adjusted version subtracts the write time from that. The cluster MTBF is the node MTBF divided by the number of nodes. Longer write time or lower MTBF changes the interval, so shortening the write pays twice.
questions.weak_answer: Picks a round interval such as every hour.
questions.follow_up: What is the interval for 8 hours MTBF and 180 seconds write?

questions.question: Asynchronous checkpointing causes host out-of-memory kills. Why and what is the fix?
questions.model_answer: The snapshot is staged in pinned host memory. If several unflushed snapshots stack up next to worker memory, the node can run out and the OOM killer fires. Allow only one snapshot in flight, wait for the previous flush before starting the next, and budget host memory for it.
questions.weak_answer: Adds swap.
questions.follow_up: What does async checkpointing do to the training pause?

questions.question: Why publish a checkpoint through a temporary directory and an atomic rename?
questions.model_answer: A crash during a direct write leaves truncated or mismatched shards in the final directory, and a restart may load them. Write into a temporary directory, flush, verify hashes, then rename it into place in one atomic step. Readers see a complete checkpoint or none.
questions.weak_answer: Writes directly and checks on load.
questions.follow_up: How would a restart choose the latest good checkpoint?

questions.question: Why reserve about 30 percent free space on a parallel file system?
questions.model_answer: Parallel file systems slow down as they fill. Extents fragment, allocator contention grows and targets become uneven near 90 percent. Keeping headroom holds steady-state fill well below that and avoids multi-minute checkpoint stalls. It also leaves room for rebuilds.
questions.weak_answer: Fills to 95 percent to save cost.
questions.follow_up: How do you size usable capacity from raw flash?

questions.question: Estimate read bandwidth for 200 MB per second per GPU on 8 GPUs, 64 GPUs and a 72-GPU rack.
questions.model_answer: Multiply per-GPU demand by the GPU count. Eight GPUs need 1.6 GB per second, 64 need 12.8 GB per second, and 72 need 14.4 GB per second. State the per-GPU assumption and add headroom for bursts and for several jobs starting together.
questions.weak_answer: Quotes the storage vendor peak figure.
questions.follow_up: Why is text pre-tokenised pretraining not read-bound?

questions.question: A checkpoint that took 90 seconds now takes 12 minutes with nothing changed in the job. What do you check?
questions.model_answer: Look at shared-file-system contention from other tenants, a single degraded storage target that slows striped writes, and a changed configuration such as stripe count or network path. Compare per-rank write times to find a slow rank or target. Check the file system's own metrics, not only the node.
questions.weak_answer: Assumes the model got bigger.
questions.follow_up: How would staggering writes or using local NVMe first help?

questions.question: Why does static training memory come to 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision, and 14 on disk?
questions.model_answer: In pure FP32 Adam, weights, gradients, momentum and variance take four bytes each, which is 16 bytes per parameter. In mixed precision, BF16 weights and gradients save space but a FP32 master copy is added, so the total is again about 16 bytes. A checkpoint stores weights and optimizer state but not gradients, which gives the 14 bytes figure the chapter uses. Activations come on top.
questions.weak_answer: Says only weights count.
questions.follow_up: What does sharding change in that budget?

questions.question: Training quality falls but nothing errors, and every epoch sees the same batch order. What did the author forget?
questions.model_answer: The distributed sampler seeds its shuffle from the seed plus the epoch. If set_epoch is never called, the epoch stays zero and every epoch uses the same shuffle. Call set_epoch at the start of each epoch. Never pass shuffle to the loader when a distributed sampler is used.
questions.weak_answer: Blames the learning rate.
questions.follow_up: What does the sampler do when the dataset does not divide evenly?

questions.question: DDP hangs when a conditional branch leaves a parameter unused. Why and what are the options?
questions.model_answer: An unused parameter never fires its gradient hook, so its bucket never becomes ready and the all-reduce never starts on some ranks. Setting find unused parameters makes DDP scan the graph every step, which costs time. If the graph is fixed, static graph is cheaper. The best fix is to make every parameter participate.
questions.weak_answer: Increases the timeout.
questions.follow_up: How do you set collective timeouts in current PyTorch?

questions.question: Compare per-GPU memory for a 70B model under DDP and the three sharding stages.
questions.model_answer: The chapter counts 12 bytes per parameter for the state, so 840 GB in all. DDP holds all of it on each GPU. Stage 1 shards the optimizer state, stage 2 also shards gradients, and stage 3 shards the weights too. Across eight GPUs that is 350, 227 and about 105 GB respectively, before activations. Larger groups cut it further.
questions.weak_answer: Says FSDP shards activations too.
questions.follow_up: What communication does stage 3 add?

questions.question: Saving an FSDP checkpoint with the default state dict crashes rank 0 with out of memory. Why?
questions.model_answer: The default full state dict gathers every shard onto rank 0. For a 70B model that is far more than one GPU can hold. Use the distributed checkpoint API with sharded state and optional CPU offload, so each rank writes its own shard.
questions.weak_answer: Adds more memory to rank 0.
questions.follow_up: How do you reload onto a different number of GPUs?

questions.question: Why did tensor parallelism of 32 across two nodes cause a large slowdown?
questions.model_answer: Tensor parallelism runs collectives on every layer. Stretching it across nodes puts those on the inter-node network instead of NVLink, so each collective is many times slower. Keep tensor parallelism inside a node, and use pipeline or data parallelism across nodes.
questions.weak_answer: Says more GPUs always means faster.
questions.follow_up: What is the pipeline bubble and how is it reduced?

questions.question: Compute the Young-Daly checkpoint interval for 8 hours MTBF and a 180-second write.
questions.model_answer: Take the square root of two times 28,800 seconds times 180 seconds, which is about 3,220 seconds. Subtract the write time of 180 seconds. The result is about 3,040 seconds, or roughly 51 minutes. The value is an estimate, so round it and review it when the failure rate changes.
questions.weak_answer: Checkpoints every 5 minutes to be safe.
questions.follow_up: How does async checkpointing change the optimum?

questions.question: Why can a try and except loop in Python not recover a distributed step when one rank dies?
questions.model_answer: Collectives need every rank in lockstep. When one rank dies, the communicator state is broken and the others hang in the collective until the watchdog fires. Recovery means tearing down the process group and restarting from a checkpoint, usually through the launcher's restart or an elastic setup.
questions.weak_answer: Catches the exception and continues.
questions.follow_up: How does elastic training change the batch size and loss behaviour?

questions.question: Why can a GPU show 100 percent utilisation and only 15 to 22 percent MFU?
questions.model_answer: Utilisation says a kernel was active, not how much of the hardware it used. Many tiny memory-bound kernels, waiting on data or communication, keep the GPU busy but do little tensor-core work. MFU compares achieved model FLOPs with the peak, so it shows real efficiency.
questions.weak_answer: Treats 100 percent as proof of efficiency.
questions.follow_up: How do you compute MFU for a 70B model on 8 H100s?

questions.question: MFU is steady at 45 percent for hours and then slides to 28 percent with no change. What do you suspect?
questions.model_answer: A slow slide points to a changing environment, not a configuration error. Thermal clock throttling is the prime suspect as temperatures rise. Check temperatures, clocks and throttle reasons, and look at data-cache decay or a growing straggler. Compare with a cool node.
questions.weak_answer: Restarts the job.
questions.follow_up: How do you tell power capping from thermal throttling?

questions.question: After a node reboot throughput drops from 950 to 310 tokens per second and all-reduce bandwidth collapses. What happened?
questions.model_answer: NCCL probably fell back from NVLink to PCIe. Typical causes are the fabric manager not starting after reboot, an NVLink that failed to train, or a BIOS setting like ACS enabled. Check the fabric manager service, the NVLink status and the NCCL topology log. Fix and re-run the bandwidth test before returning the node.
questions.weak_answer: Retunes the batch size.
questions.follow_up: Which test proves the node is healthy again?

questions.question: Why does LLM inference need a KV cache and training does not?
questions.model_answer: In training the whole target sequence is known, so attention over all tokens runs in one parallel pass. In generation the tokens come one at a time. Without a cache, every new token would recompute keys and values for all earlier tokens. The cache stores them, so each step computes only the new token. The cost is memory that grows with context length and batch size.
strong_answer_contains: Parallel training pass versus sequential generation
questions.weak_answer: Says the cache stores the model outputs for repeat questions.
questions.follow_up: How do you compute the cache size per token?

questions.question: Give the per-token KV cache formula and explain why Llama-3-70B uses about 8 times less than a 70B model with full multi-head attention.
questions.model_answer: Per token it is two, for keys and values, times the layer count, times the number of key-value heads, times the head dimension, times bytes per element. Llama-3-70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads instead of 64, so the cache is one eighth. That allows many more concurrent sequences.
strong_answer_contains: Formula with the factor of two
questions.weak_answer: Says the 70B model is just smaller.
questions.follow_up: What does doubling tensor parallelism do to the number of sequences that fit?

questions.question: Why does 4-bit weight quantisation win at low concurrency and 8-bit with 8-bit activations win at high concurrency?
questions.model_answer: At low concurrency decode is limited by memory bandwidth, so smaller weights help most. At high concurrency or long prefill the work becomes compute-bound, and 8-bit math units give more compute throughput than 4-bit weights that must be dequantised. Always check accuracy on your task too.
questions.weak_answer: Says 4-bit is always faster.
questions.follow_up: When is quantisation-aware training needed?

questions.question: How does PagedAttention reduce memory waste?
questions.model_answer: It splits the KV cache into small fixed-size blocks and maps each sequence's logical blocks to any free physical block through a block table. There is no need for contiguous memory, so external fragmentation disappears, and waste is limited to the last partly filled block. More sequences fit, which raises throughput.
strong_answer_contains: Fixed blocks and a block table
Waste bounded to the last block
questions.weak_answer: Describes it as a faster attention kernel.
questions.follow_up: How does prefix caching reuse blocks?

questions.question: Which metrics do you watch on every production vLLM deployment?
questions.model_answer: Cache usage, because high values lead to preemption. Preemption count. Queue depth and running requests. Time to first token and time per output token. GPU health from DCGM. The chapter gives example thresholds, for instance alerting on cache usage above 95 percent for two minutes, so treat them as starting points for your own load.
questions.weak_answer: Watches only GPU utilisation.
questions.follow_up: Why must swap space be zero for latency-critical serving?

questions.question: Define goodput. Why did the colocated GPU in the DistServe example reach 3 RPS on TTFT yet only 1.6 RPS goodput?
questions.model_answer: Goodput counts only requests that meet both the time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token targets. When prefill and decode share a GPU, long prompts delay running decodes, so the per-token target is missed even when first-token latency is fine. Counting only requests that meet both targets gives 1.6.
questions.weak_answer: Quotes raw throughput as the headline number.
questions.follow_up: How does separating prefill and decode change goodput?

questions.question: Chunked prefill exists. Why might you still disaggregate prefill and decode?
questions.model_answer: Even with chunking, a prefill chunk in the same batch stretches every step, which delays all decode streams during prompt ingestion. Very small chunks add overhead. Separate pools let each phase use its own parallelism and hardware and be scaled on its own. The cost is moving the KV cache over the network, so it pays off for long prompts and strict latency targets.
questions.weak_answer: Says disaggregation is always better.
questions.follow_up: How do you size the prefill-to-decode ratio?

questions.question: How do you size the ratio of prefill workers to decode workers?
questions.model_answer: Prefill workers equal arrival rate times uncached input tokens divided by prefill throughput, rounded up. Decode workers equal arrival rate times output tokens divided by decode throughput. The ratio follows the input-to-output token ratio and the throughput ratio. Chat, retrieval and reasoning workloads therefore need different ratios.
questions.weak_answer: Splits the GPUs evenly.
questions.follow_up: Why must you use uncached input tokens?

questions.question: Why do commercial APIs price output tokens higher, and how do TTFT and inter-token latency differ?
questions.model_answer: Time to first token is set by prefill, which is compute-bound. Inter-token latency is set by decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound and handles one token per step per sequence. Decode uses the GPU less efficiently per token, so output tokens cost more. Targets also differ, with first-token targets in hundreds of milliseconds for chat.
questions.weak_answer: Says output is pricier only because it is longer.
questions.follow_up: How do you compute end-to-end latency from these?

questions.question: Why does a closed-loop load test hide overload, and what should you use?
questions.model_answer: A closed-loop test has a fixed number of clients, each waiting for its reply before sending the next request. When the server slows, the arrival rate drops automatically, so queues never build and the test looks healthy. An open-loop test sends at a set rate regardless of replies and shows the queue and the tail growing. Use it to find the real limit.
questions.weak_answer: Reports the average latency at a fixed concurrency.
questions.follow_up: Which tool flags control the load pattern?

questions.question: How do you stop 503 errors when a model pod is terminated or reloaded?
questions.model_answer: First fail the readiness check so the pod is removed from endpoints. Then wait in a pre-stop hook long enough for the proxies to notice, and give the engine a long grace period to finish streams. Use a disruption budget for planned changes. Test it with a streaming load while rolling the deployment.
questions.weak_answer: Raises the replica count only.
questions.follow_up: What about requests that stream for five minutes?

questions.question: How do you turn hourly hardware cost and throughput into a cost per million tokens?
questions.model_answer: Divide the total hourly cost, hardware plus operations, by the millions of tokens produced per hour at realised utilisation. Tokens per second times 3,600 divided by a million gives millions per hour. Use realised utilisation, not peak, and count only tokens that meet your latency targets.
questions.weak_answer: Uses vendor peak throughput.
questions.follow_up: Why does doubling tensor parallelism more than double concurrent sequences?

questions.question: What makes ML data harder to version than code, and what is the minimum versioning contract?
questions.model_answer: Datasets are large, they change by appends and repartitioning, and models inherit each other's data bugs. Git cannot hold them. Use content-addressed storage plus a small record per dataset: dataset id, content hash, source, snapshot time, row count, schema hash, storage path, parents and retention date. The id is the address and the hash is the proof.
questions.weak_answer: Says put the dataset in Git LFS and tag it.
questions.follow_up: How does a training script refer to a dataset?

questions.question: The overall AUC is flat but one customer segment got much worse. How does a promotion gate catch that?
questions.model_answer: The gate reads per-segment metrics from the run record and refuses promotion when any segment drops by more than a set limit. The overall number can hide a sharp fall in one slice, so the gate checks slices, not just the average.
questions.weak_answer: Trusts the overall metric.

questions.question: Why treat the training image as a release artefact?
questions.model_answer: The training environment is part of the supply chain. Build the image once, sign it, and store it in a registry that checks signatures. The pipeline refuses to start training from an unsigned image. Then a model's lineage includes a known, reproducible environment.
questions.weak_answer: Builds the image at the start of each job.

questions.question: Why stage the previous model for rollback in advance?
questions.model_answer: Rollback happens under time pressure, so you want a tag change, not a model download or rebuild. Keep the previous version warm in the registry, in object storage and in the cluster's image cache. The cost is one extra artefact. Test the rollback path regularly.

questions.question: What does a lineage record contain, and what question does it answer?
questions.model_answer: It holds the dataset snapshot id, the code commit, the environment image hash, and the parent model and run ids. It answers which data, code and environment produced this model, and which earlier version it came from. That supports audits, reproduction and the decision to roll back.

questions.question: What biases does an LLM judge have, and how do you reduce them?
questions.model_answer: A judge model can prefer answers in its own style, prefer the first of two answers, prefer longer answers, and anchor on earlier scores. Reduce the bias with a different model family for the judge, a randomised answer order, length controls, and spot checks by humans. Do not treat judge scores as ground truth.
questions.weak_answer: Treats the judge as ground truth.

questions.question: Why is the regression set more important than the golden set?
questions.model_answer: The golden set measures overall quality on a sample. The regression set holds known failure cases, so a change that breaks one of them is caught even if the average looks fine. Its value depends on coverage, so add every production failure to it.
questions.weak_answer: Says the golden set is enough.

questions.question: What is the difference between feature drift and concept drift?
questions.model_answer: Feature drift means the input distribution changed while the relation between inputs and target did not. Concept drift means the relation itself changed even if inputs look the same. Input monitoring catches the first. Performance monitoring, which needs labels, catches the second.
questions.weak_answer: Treats them as the same thing.

questions.question: What is the population stability index and what are its limits as a drift alert?
questions.model_answer: It compares two histograms and returns one number, is cheap, and works on binned numeric and categorical features. The thresholds in the chapter, 0.2 to page and 0.5 to consider rollback, are the chapter's example values and not universal. Set your own from history, and pair it with a performance signal.

questions.question: Name the retraining trigger types and when each is right.
questions.model_answer: Schedule-based retraining runs every fixed period and suits stable domains. Drift-triggered retraining fires when a drift detector crosses a threshold and suits fast-changing inputs. Performance-triggered retraining fires when live accuracy falls and needs labels. Add a cooldown so triggers cannot cause a retrain loop, and always produce a new model version.
questions.weak_answer: Retrains on every alert.
