questions.question: Explain a multi-window, multi-burn-rate alert for a 99.5 percent 30-day SLO.
questions.model_answer: The error budget is 0.5 percent of requests over the window. A burn rate of one uses exactly the whole budget by the end of the window. A burn rate of 14.4 uses it in about two days, so you page when it holds over both a long window and a short one, for example one hour and five minutes. The long window shows it matters and the short one shows it is still happening. Slower burns raise a ticket instead.
questions.weak_answer: Alerts on any error above the SLO.
questions.follow_up: What does a burn rate of 6 over six hours mean?

questions.question: In Alertmanager, what do grouping, inhibition and silences do, and what is a watchdog alert?
questions.model_answer: Grouping collapses many alerts from one outage into one notification. Inhibition suppresses symptom alerts while a root-cause alert is firing. A silence mutes alerts for a set time, usually during planned work. A watchdog alert fires all the time, so its absence tells you the alerting pipeline itself is broken.
questions.weak_answer: Says to delete noisy alerts.
questions.follow_up: How would you reduce 500 alerts a day?

questions.question: Why must you not put request ids or user ids into Loki stream labels?
questions.model_answer: Loki indexes only the stream labels and keeps the log lines compressed in object storage. A label with unbounded values creates a huge number of streams and ruins both the index and the query speed. Keep labels few and stable, and search the id with a line filter or structured metadata.
questions.weak_answer: Adds every field as a label for easy search.
questions.follow_up: How do exemplars link a metric to a trace?

questions.question: What causes a Prometheus cardinality explosion and how do you stop it quickly?
questions.model_answer: Series count is the product of the distinct values of all labels. One unbounded label, like a user id or a raw URL path, multiplies it. Find the culprit with the top-series queries on the server, then drop or relabel the label at scrape time, or normalise the path. Fix the source in code afterwards.
strong_answer_contains: Relabel at scrape then fix source
questions.weak_answer: Restarts Prometheus to free memory.
questions.follow_up: How would you budget cardinality in advance?

questions.question: What is an error budget and how is it used?
questions.model_answer: The error budget is the SLO turned into an allowance. At 99.9 percent monthly availability it is about 43 minutes in a 30-day month. The team spends it on releases, experiments and upgrades, and slows change down when it is used up. It turns reliability into a shared decision.
questions.weak_answer: Says it is the number of incidents allowed.
questions.follow_up: How does burn rate relate to it?

questions.question: Define RTO and RPO and say why they must be agreed with the business.
questions.model_answer: The recovery time objective is how long a service may be down after a disaster. The recovery point objective is how much data you may lose. They set cost, because shorter targets need replication and standby capacity. The chapter gives example tiers, but the real values come from the business and must be tested.
questions.weak_answer: Says RPO is how fast you recover.
questions.follow_up: What does a restore drill measure?

questions.question: Why do immutable or object-locked backups matter against ransomware?
questions.model_answer: Object lock prevents deletion before the retention period ends, so an attacker with credentials cannot delete the backups. A separate account or an air-gapped copy adds more protection. Backups are only useful if you test the restore.
questions.weak_answer: Relies on daily backups in the same account.
questions.follow_up: What does a DR game day cover?

questions.question: What do MTTA, MTTM and MTTR measure, and which matters most to users?
questions.model_answer: Mean time to acknowledge is alert to human response. Mean time to mitigate is alert to reduced impact. Mean time to resolve is alert to full fix. Users feel the time to mitigate most, so a runbook that gets to a safe state quickly matters more than a perfect fix.
questions.weak_answer: Optimises MTTR only.

questions.question: Compare N+1 and 2N redundancy.
questions.model_answer: N+1 keeps one spare for every N needed components and the spare takes over on failure. 2N keeps two full sets running together. N+1 costs less and 2N gives higher availability and simpler failover. Choose by how long you can afford to be down and how much the capacity costs.
questions.weak_answer: Picks 2N for everything.

questions.question: What do the three Pod Security Standards profiles allow, and how is Pod Security Admission turned on for a namespace?
questions.model_answer: Privileged is unrestricted and is for trusted system components. Baseline blocks known host escapes such as host networking, privileged containers and host paths. Restricted adds hardening such as non-root users and dropped capabilities. You apply them with labels on the namespace that set enforce, audit and warn modes. Start with audit and warn, then enforce.
questions.weak_answer: Says it is a per-pod setting inside the pod spec only.
questions.follow_up: Which namespaces would need privileged?

questions.question: GPU RDMA pods need IPC_LOCK. How do you fit that with the restricted profile?
questions.model_answer: Restricted does not allow extra capabilities, and baseline does not include IPC_LOCK. Do not relax the whole cluster. Run RDMA training in a dedicated namespace with a documented exception, or raise the memlock limit through the runtime so the capability is not needed, and back it with admission policy that limits who can use it.
questions.weak_answer: Runs the pods as privileged.
questions.follow_up: What else does a pinned-memory limit control?

questions.question: Why should a multi-tenant cluster deny tenant pods that set nodeName?
questions.model_answer: A pod with nodeName set skips the scheduler and is bound straight to that node. A tenant could then avoid taints, quota checks and node selectors and land on a dedicated or control-plane node. An admission rule that denies nodeName on tenant pods closes this path.
questions.weak_answer: Says taints are enough.
questions.follow_up: What other fields let a pod escape the intended placement?

questions.question: Explain keyless image signing in CI and the policy mistake that defeats it.
questions.model_answer: The CI job gets a short-lived identity token from its provider. A certificate authority issues a short-lived certificate tied to that identity, the image is signed, and the signature goes to a transparency log. Verification must pin the identity, meaning the repository and workflow. If the policy only checks that some valid signature exists, anyone with an account can sign an image and pass.
questions.weak_answer: Says a valid signature is enough.
questions.follow_up: How do you verify initContainers and ephemeral containers too?

questions.question: Why is loading a PyTorch checkpoint with the default loader risky, and what are safer options?
questions.model_answer: Those files are Python pickle streams. A pickle can name any callable to run on load, so loading an untrusted file can execute code. Safer options are weight-only loading modes, tensor formats that carry no code such as safetensors, and verifying signatures or hashes of model files. Treat third-party weights as untrusted input.
questions.weak_answer: Says weights are just data.
questions.follow_up: What does trust_remote_code do in model loading?

questions.question: What controls does a multi-tenant notebook service on a GPU cluster need?
questions.model_answer: Notebooks run whatever users type, so treat them as untrusted. Use restricted pod security, non-root users, resource quotas and idle culling, default-deny network policy with controlled egress, no cluster credentials in the pod, scoped storage, and audit logging. Add GPU limits so one user cannot hold the cluster.
questions.weak_answer: Trusts users because they are employees.
questions.follow_up: Which GPU sharing mode do you use for notebooks and why?

questions.question: Which three isolation pillars let departments share a GPU cluster?
questions.model_answer: Compute isolation, using MIG slices or dedicated nodes with taints. Network isolation, using default-deny network policies and, on the fabric, partitioning such as SR-IOV virtual functions and partition keys. Storage isolation, using separate volumes or paths with quotas and access control. Add audit logging so you can prove it. The chapter's customer scenario is a worked example.
questions.weak_answer: Relies on namespaces alone.
questions.follow_up: What does MIG isolate and what does it share?

questions.question: Why does egress filtering matter as much as ingress on GPU nodes?
questions.model_answer: If a container or dependency is compromised, the attacker needs to call home, fetch more tools and send out data such as model weights or datasets. Default-deny egress with an allow list stops those steps even if the first break-in succeeds. Registry and package access go through controlled proxies.
questions.weak_answer: Says the firewall at the edge is enough.
questions.follow_up: How do you let nodes reach a registry safely?

questions.question: How does InfiniBand partitioning isolate tenants?
questions.model_answer: The subnet manager programs partition keys into each port. Traffic is accepted only between ports that share a key, and full or limited membership controls who can talk to whom. It is enforced by the hardware, so it isolates tenants on the fabric below IP. Protect the subnet manager and management keys too.
questions.weak_answer: Says use VLANs on the IB network.
questions.follow_up: How do BlueField DPUs add to this isolation?

questions.question: List the Linux capability sets and say why CAP_SYS_ADMIN is called the new root.
questions.model_answer: Each thread has permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding and ambient sets. Effective is what the kernel checks. The bounding set limits what can ever be gained. CAP_SYS_ADMIN covers a very broad set of privileged operations, so granting it is nearly the same as granting root. Give containers the smallest set they need, and inspect them with the proc status fields.
questions.weak_answer: Says capabilities are the same as UIDs.
questions.follow_up: How do seccomp and AppArmor add to capabilities?

questions.question: How does Slurm backfill let small jobs run without starving a large multi-node job?
questions.model_answer: When the top job cannot start, backfill uses the time limits of running jobs to work out the earliest time the large job can start and reserves nodes for it from then. It then starts lower-priority jobs only if they finish before that time. Accurate time limits on small jobs make backfill work, so very loose limits hurt everyone.
strong_answer_contains: Fits only jobs that end in time
questions.weak_answer: Says backfill just runs small jobs whenever there is space.
questions.follow_up: Which scheduler parameters tune the backfill window?

questions.question: A researcher says their job is stuck in PENDING. How do you read the reason?
questions.model_answer: Show the reason with squeue for that job, then match it. Priority means higher-priority jobs are ahead, so look at the priority factors and fairshare. Resources means it is at the top and waiting for nodes. A limit reason such as an association group limit means a quota is hit. A node-not-available reason points to a reservation or a drained node. A time-limit reason means the request exceeds the partition limit.
strong_answer_contains: Checks the right tool for each
questions.weak_answer: Tells the user to resubmit.
questions.follow_up: How do you check fairshare for the account?

questions.question: Compare --gres=gpu:4, --gpus-per-node=4, --gpus=8 and --gpus-per-task=1 for a 2-node job.
questions.model_answer: The first two ask for four GPUs on each node, which is eight in total and symmetric, which suits NCCL. Asking for eight GPUs for the job lets Slurm pack them unevenly, which can hurt collectives. GPUs per task ties GPUs to ranks. State nodes, GPUs, CPUs and tasks explicitly in batch scripts.
questions.weak_answer: Treats them as identical.
questions.follow_up: How do GPU binding options change rank placement?

questions.question: After a reboot a node is drained with gres/gpu count too low. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.model_answer: slurmd may have started before the driver, the NVML library or the MIG layout was ready, or a GPU may have dropped off the bus, which shows as an Xid in the kernel log. Check that all GPUs appear in nvidia-smi, fix the cause, and order the services so slurmd starts after the GPU stack. Resume the node only after a health check passes.
questions.weak_answer: Resumes the node straight away.
questions.follow_up: How does a health-check program help?

questions.question: What happens to a node and its job when a prolog or epilog fails?
questions.model_answer: If the prolog fails, the node is drained and the job is requeued, and held unless a parameter says otherwise. If the epilog fails, the node is drained. This is useful, because a node with a broken environment stops taking jobs. It also means a flaky script can drain many nodes, so test them and keep them short.
questions.weak_answer: Believes failed prologs are ignored.
questions.follow_up: How should an epilog clean up user processes safely?

questions.question: Compare DRAINING, DRAINED and DOWN. When do you use drain and when down?
questions.model_answer: Draining marks a node so it takes no new jobs while running jobs finish. Drained means the node is empty and stays out until resumed. Down means the node is unusable now. Use drain for planned work or a suspect node, so running jobs can complete. Use down when the node is dead or must be treated as lost.
questions.weak_answer: Says they are the same.
questions.follow_up: What does ReturnToService do?

questions.question: slurmctld crashes during a large run. What happens to running jobs?
questions.model_answer: Running jobs keep going, because the step daemon on each node manages them. New jobs cannot start and commands fail or block until the controller returns. Completion messages queue on the nodes. With a standby controller, takeover needs the shared state directory to be reachable and consistent. If slurmdbd is down the controller keeps a cache and queues accounting records.
questions.weak_answer: Says all jobs are killed.
questions.follow_up: Why is the state directory the real single point of failure?

questions.question: Why must Pyxis be rebuilt when Slurm is upgraded?
questions.model_answer: Pyxis is a plug-in that links against Slurm internals. Those change across major releases, so a plug-in built for an older release will not load. Include the rebuild and redeploy in the upgrade plan, and hold the Slurm packages from automatic updates.
questions.weak_answer: Upgrades Slurm and sees if jobs fail.
questions.follow_up: What is the correct upgrade order for Slurm components?

questions.question: Why does a one-scalable-unit DGX B200 SuperPOD have 31 servers and not 32?
questions.model_answer: In the reference design a management appliance for the fabric takes the place of one server in the first unit. So the counts are 31, 63, 95 and 127 for one to four units. Quote the reference document for your exact generation and check the current version.
questions.weak_answer: Says nodes are missing or faulty.
questions.follow_up: What is the partial-unit fabric rule?

questions.question: Which port and authentication does the Base Command Manager daemon use for cmsh and the web GUI?
questions.model_answer: The management daemon accepts connections over SSL on port 8081, set in its configuration file. Clients authenticate with X.509 client certificates kept under the administrator's home directory. The plain port is used only during initial setup. Check your version's documentation before relying on the numbers.
questions.weak_answer: Says it uses a shared password.
questions.follow_up: Where do you see node state in BCM?

questions.question: Five jobs ask for 8, 4, 4, 8 and 4 GPUs on 8-GPU nodes. How many nodes with and without bin-packing?
questions.model_answer: Without packing, one job per node needs five nodes and uses 28 of 40 GPUs, which is 70 percent. With packing, the two 4-GPU jobs share a node, and the third 4-GPU job takes its own, so four nodes are enough with 28 of 32 GPUs, which is 87.5 percent. Packing improves utilisation, but it needs isolation between jobs on one node.
questions.weak_answer: Gives one node per job without checking packing.
questions.follow_up: How does GPU fragmentation arise in the default scheduler?

questions.question: Nominal capacity is 100,000 tokens per second, with 40 percent utilisation and 80 percent availability. What is effective capacity and why use it?
questions.model_answer: Effective capacity is nominal times expected utilisation times availability, so 100,000 times 0.4 times 0.8 is 32,000 tokens per second. It is what you can plan around. Quote the assumptions, since utilisation and availability are the numbers most often wrong.
questions.weak_answer: Plans on the nominal figure.
questions.follow_up: Which of the three numbers would you measure first?

questions.question: Walk through a three-year TCO and cost per GPU-year for a staged build.
questions.model_answer: Add capital cost for each stage and operating cost for each year to get total cost. Count active GPU-years as GPUs times years in service per stage. Divide. In the chapter's example, 464 GPUs in year one plus 60 and 100 later give 1,612 GPU-years, and the total of 28.8 million dollars gives about 17.9 thousand dollars per GPU-year. State that the inputs are the chapter's example.
questions.weak_answer: Divides the purchase price by three.
questions.follow_up: What changes if GPUs are leased?

questions.question: Self-hosting costs $12.40 an hour for 2,100 tokens per second at peak. A managed API costs $4 per million tokens. What is the break-even?
questions.model_answer: At full use the replica makes 7.56 million tokens an hour, so it costs about $1.64 per million. Divided by the API price, break-even utilisation is about 41 percent. That is roughly 74 million tokens a day. Below that volume the API is cheaper. Include operations cost and the latency targets.
questions.weak_answer: Says self-hosting is always cheaper.
questions.follow_up: How would burstiness change the answer?

questions.question: Soft and hard multi-tenancy in Kubernetes: which do you build and when?
questions.model_answer: Soft multi-tenancy assumes cooperating teams and protects against accidents. It uses namespaces, quotas, RBAC, network policy and admission rules in one cluster. Hard multi-tenancy assumes hostile tenants and needs stronger boundaries such as separate clusters, virtual clusters or isolated node pools and hardware isolation. Choose by the trust level and compliance needs, and say what you give up in cost.
questions.weak_answer: Says namespaces are enough for any tenant.
questions.follow_up: How would you offer GPU quotas to many teams?

questions.question: Design GPU queueing for three teams with guaranteed shares and borrowing.
questions.model_answer: Define resource flavours for hardware tiers, a namespaced local queue per team, and a cluster queue per team with a nominal quota. Put the queues in a cohort so unused quota can be borrowed, with limits for borrowing and lending. Add priorities and preemption rules, gang admission for multi-node jobs and a clear policy for fairness. Monitor wait time per queue.
questions.weak_answer: Uses a namespace quota per team.
questions.follow_up: What happens when a lender needs its quota back?

questions.question: GPUs sit idle during distributed training. How do you separate host CPU, storage and parallelism or network causes?
questions.model_answer: Check host CPU first, because decode or tokenisation can peg the cores. If CPUs are idle and I/O wait is high, storage is the limit. If both are fine, look at communication: the share of step time in collectives, and whether the parallel layout fits the topology. Take one measurement at a time and change one thing.
questions.weak_answer: Adds more GPUs.
questions.follow_up: Which tools do you use for each check?

questions.question: How do you size a training cluster from a model size and a time target?
questions.model_answer: Start from the model and token budget to get total compute, then from the achieved utilisation to get GPU-hours, then from the deadline to get GPU count. Add the node count, the network design to fit it, the checkpoint size and write bandwidth, and failure and restart overhead. State each assumption and give a range. Verify with a small run before you commit.
questions.weak_answer: Names a cluster size from experience.
questions.follow_up: What would you measure in a pilot?

questions.question: What does a good 128-GPU cluster TCO comparison between InfiniBand and Ethernet need to include?
questions.model_answer: Include the capital cost of nodes, fabric, racks and install, plus yearly power, support and staff. Convert to a cost per GPU-hour. Then add the cost of lost throughput from a slower fabric, since a small percent loss of a large cluster is large money. Be honest that vendor price and performance inputs are assumptions to verify.
questions.weak_answer: Compares only switch prices.
questions.follow_up: How would a pilot cluster settle the question?

questions.question: How do you make a proof of concept falsifiable?
questions.model_answer: Write down, before the test, the numeric result that would count as failure, for example a latency percentile at a given load. Without it the proof of concept is a demo. Agree the measure, the data and the owner with the customer in advance, and report against that line.
questions.weak_answer: Runs a demo and asks if the customer is happy.
questions.follow_up: Why measure p95 or p99 and not the average?

questions.question: Describe the stages of your architecture method when a customer asks for a design.
questions.model_answer: Discover the requirements and constraints. Model the data and request path, control, trust, state, failure domains and observability. Compare options with their trade-offs. Recommend one and say why. Validate with a falsifiable test. Adopt with a plan for operation. Keep requirements, assumptions, constraints and trade-offs separate in the write-up.
questions.weak_answer: Jumps to a product list.
questions.follow_up: Which stage do people most often skip?

questions.question: Tell me about an incident you led. How do you structure your answer?
questions.model_answer: Use situation, impact, detection, actions and result. Name your role, whether commander or responder, and what you decided. Give the timeline and the mitigation before the root cause. Say what you changed afterward and what the follow-up items were. Do not invent numbers, and be honest about what went badly.
questions.weak_answer: Tells a story where nothing went wrong.
questions.follow_up: What would you do differently?

questions.question: What are the core elements of a blameless post-incident review?
questions.model_answer: A factual timeline, the impact, the contributing factors and the detection gap. It asks how the system allowed the error, not who made it. It lists action items with owners and dates, and it records what went well. Share it widely. Without follow-through on the items, the review changes nothing.
questions.weak_answer: Names the engineer at fault.
questions.follow_up: How do you track action items to completion?

questions.question: A customer asks for a cluster design, but their requirements are vague. What do you do first?
questions.model_answer: Ask questions to find the workload, scale, deadlines, data size, security and budget. Write down what you learn as requirements and what you assume as assumptions. Offer two or three options with trade-offs, and propose a small test. Do not promise numbers you cannot support. Leave an action list at the end of the meeting.
questions.weak_answer: Presents a favourite architecture at once.
questions.follow_up: How do you handle a requirement that cannot be met?

questions.question: Describe a time you pushed back on a risky change. How do you frame it?
questions.model_answer: State the risk in terms of impact and likelihood and tie it to a measure such as the error budget. Offer a safer path, for example a canary or a staged rollout. Agree on what evidence would change your mind. Keep it about the system, then accept the decision and help with the rollout. Use a real example only.
questions.weak_answer: Says no without an alternative.
questions.follow_up: What if you were overruled and it failed?

questions.question: How do you explain GPU cost and utilisation to a non-technical executive?
questions.model_answer: Use one measure they can act on, such as cost per useful GPU-hour or cost per million tokens. Separate allocated from used. Show where the gap is, for example idle reservations, and what each fix would save. Avoid jargon, say what you are unsure of, and end with a decision you need from them.
questions.weak_answer: Shows a wall of dashboards.
questions.follow_up: How would chargeback change team behaviour?

questions.question: What do you do when you do not know the answer in an interview?
questions.model_answer: Say what you do know and what you would check. Give the first measurement you would take. State your assumptions out loud and ask a clarifying question. A clear reasoning path scores better than a guess. Never invent a number or a flag. The Volume 20 chapters on the final round and the cheat sheet give practice for this.
